lesson.title: Undoing the Square Directly
lesson.summary: When a quadratic equation has no linear term, or can be written as a squared expression equal to a number, you can solve it directly by taking the square root of both sides.
lesson.body:
Some quadratic equations do not need the full machinery of factoring or a formula. If a quadratic equation can be arranged so that a squared quantity sits alone on one side, you can solve it by undoing the square directly, the same way you would undo any operation, by applying its inverse to both sides. The inverse of squaring is taking a square root, but there is one detail that makes quadratics behave differently from linear equations: both a positive and a negative number square to the same positive result. So when you take the square root of both sides of x^2 = k, you must remember both possibilities, x = sqrt(k) and x = -sqrt(k), usually written together as x = plus or minus the square root of k.

Start with the simplest case, a quadratic with no linear term at all, like 2x^2 - 8 = 0. Isolate the squared term first: 2x^2 = 8, then x^2 = 4. Taking the square root of both sides gives x = plus or minus the square root of 4, so x = 2 or x = -2. Checking both: 2(2)^2 - 8 = 8 - 8 = 0, and 2(-2)^2 - 8 = 8 - 8 = 0. Both work, because squaring erases the sign.

The same idea extends to a squared binomial. Consider (x - 3)^2 = 16. Taking the square root of both sides gives x - 3 = plus or minus 4. Splitting into two equations, x - 3 = 4 gives x = 7, and x - 3 = -4 gives x = -1. Checking both in the original equation: (7 - 3)^2 = 4^2 = 16, and (-1 - 3)^2 = (-4)^2 = 16. Both check out.

You do need to watch the sign on the right side before you take a square root. If the equation reads (x + 2)^2 = -9, there is no real number whose square is negative, so this equation has no real solution. That is not a mistake, it is useful information, and it is the first hint of a theme that returns when the quadratic formula produces a negative number under its radical.

It is worth noticing that solving by square roots and solving by graphing are really the same question asked two ways. The equation (x - 3)^2 - 16 = 0 describes a parabola with vertex (3, -16), and the x intercepts you would read off that graph are exactly x = 7 and x = -1, the same answers found algebraically above. The square root method just gets you there exactly, without needing to sketch anything.
